world.bio: Australian, born in Newcastle NSW, sixty-eight. I examined IELTS speaking for twenty years across Asia: Hanoi, Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, Seoul, and finally Ho Chi Minh City, where I retired to Thao Dien three years ago. Six weeks ago I had a total knee replacement. I'm recovering, restless, and bored stiff. I'm writing a memoir nobody asked for and watching cricket at 3am.
skills_assets: Examined IELTS speaking for twenty years across Asia
Calibrated examiner training: know exactly what band 6, 7 and 8 sound like and how to coach for each
Fluent with the typical errors of Vietnamese, Thai, Korean and Chinese learners
A flat in Thao Dien with a spare room, a good internet connection and a standing desk
A small network of expat teachers and a couple of Vietnamese university lecturers I trust
A stack of past speaking test cue cards and examiner notes I'm allowed to keep
Can role-play a wide range of examinee personalities, from the over-rehearsed to the very shy, for training purposes
Familiar with the public band descriptors and what separates a 6.5 from a 7 in coherence and lexical resource

projects.name: Knee rehab
projects.text: Knee replacement six weeks ago at a private hospital in District 2. The surgery itself went well. The hospital's home nurse costs $40 a visit and I need dressings changed twice a week for another three weeks, then a check-up. That's $80 a week for dressings alone, on top of physio. My insurer is dragging its feet on the claim, and I've been told eight to twelve weeks. The surgeon, Dr Hieu, is excellent, quiet and quick, with a good sense of humour about foreigners who refuse to do their exercises. He wants me at ninety degrees flexion by the check-up on the twelfth. I'm at eighty-two. My physio says the stiffness is normal, but I lie awake doing the maths of whether I'll make it.

projects.name: Memoir
projects.text: I'm 31,000 words into something called 'Forty Thousand Candidates.' It's about the odd intimacy of examining: you spend eleven minutes with a stranger and you see exactly where they are afraid. I have a chapter on a Korean boy who froze at Part 2 and a chapter on a Thai grandmother who aced it. I don't know who will publish it. I'm not sure it matters. I'm trying to write in the mornings, which is when the knee hurts less. Chapter nineteen is about the examiner's duty to stay neutral when someone is clearly in distress. I once examined a young man whose father had died the day before. He sat through the whole test without mentioning it. I gave him a 7.5. I've never forgotten his hands.

projects.name: Speaking partner for local students
projects.text: A friend teaching at a university in Thu Duc told me her students are desperate for native speaking practice, especially ones who need IELTS 6.5 for study abroad. I said I'd think about doing a weekly half-hour chat. I haven't committed. I'm not sure I'm up for it while I'm still hobbling. Lan thinks twice a week would be too much for me now, so she's suggested once a week for thirty minutes via video, students rotating. I like the idea of having something regular. The problem is I'm in a flat on the sixth floor of a building with a slow lift and a knee that doesn't love stairs. Video suits.

notes.text: Six weeks post-op. Walked to the end of the lane and back, 400 metres. A motorbike nearly took me out at the crossing. The physio says to build up. I say I'd like to build up without dying.

Dressing change at 4 pm. The nurse, Trang, is lovely and very efficient but each visit is $40 and she can only come twice a week. The wound looks clean. She says another three weeks. I did the sum again. $240 more. I can pay it, but I don't enjoy it.

Cricket at 3am. England collapsed in the afternoon session, as expected. I fell asleep during the tea break and missed the whole third day. Woke at dawn on the sofa with the dog staring at me. Not a good look.

Another bad night. Woke at 2.40 with the leg throbbing and lay there counting Vietnamese tones: ma, má, mà, mả, mã, mạ. Six words, one syllable. Twenty years of examining speakers who struggled with English and I still can't say 'ma' without the woman at the market laughing. Eventually I turned the cricket on mute and watched the lights from the street move across the ceiling.

Wrote the chapter about the Thai grandmother. She was seventy-one, sitting an IELTS speaking test to join her son in Melbourne. She had learned English from a radio. She got a 7. I remember her sitting very straight at the end and saying, 'Thank you, sir. I will see my grandchildren now.' I went to the loo afterwards and had a quiet cry.

The insurer rejected the first claim form because of a missing stamp. I've spent four hours on the phone being transferred between departments with names like 'International Claims Resolution'. I spent twenty years deciding who's fluent. Now I'm learning what it feels like to be on the other end of a bad conversation.

The physio came and made me do stairs. Up two steps, down two steps, ten times. She said I did very well and I said it felt like running a marathon. She said in six weeks you will run for a bus. I said I haven't run for a bus since 1994. She wrote that down as a goal anyway.

Hung out with Lan, the lecturer from Thu Duc. She wants me to come to a class and do a mock test for her students. I said not yet, I can't stand for forty minutes. She said then sit. I said then I'll think about it.

Walked 600 metres. A small victory. Bought a coconut from the street vendor, who knows me now as 'Mr Graham, new knee.' He asked if I could still dance. I said I've never been able to. He laughed so hard he nearly dropped the coconut.

Looked through old cue cards for Part 2. 'Describe a person who has helped you.' I sat and thought of Trang with her dressing kit and her patience. If I'd drawn that card in a test, I'd have spoken for two minutes without notes. That's the thing about speaking tests: when it's real, you don't need to remember what to say.

Finished a draft of the Korean boy chapter. He froze at Part 2, then I gave him a prompt about his favourite food, and he cried because it was his mother's kimchi stew. He scored a 6.5. I don't know whether he got into his university. I'll never know.

The swelling is down. The surgeon's check-up is on the 12th. The nurse said no more dressings after that, if all goes well. Meanwhile I'm still bored. If someone would just ask me to examine something, anything, I'd happily do it sitting down.

The neighbour's son came round, Khoa, seventeen, polite as a bishop, nervous as a cat. He wants a 7.0 for Sydney. We did Part 1 and Part 3. His fluency is fine. His answers are the problem: he says 'I think it is good' about everything. I said, tell me one thing you don't like about your school. He went red and said, 'Is it allowed?' I said, yes, you're allowed to be honest. He talked for ninety seconds without stopping.

messages.text:
Lan: Graham, are you walking yet?
Me: A little. Not enough to be useful.
Lan: My students would love a conversation with you.
Me: Ask me when I can stand for forty minutes.

Trang: Mr Graham, Thursday 4 pm for dressing?
Me: Perfect. I'll make tea.
Trang: Please keep the leg elevated.
Me: Yes, nurse.

Insurer: Your claim has been received. Please allow 8-12 weeks.
Me: I submitted it six weeks ago.
Insurer: Please allow 8-12 weeks.
Me: I understand. Thank you.

Sophie: Dad, are you eating properly?
Me: Yes. I'm having noodles every day.
Sophie: That's not what I meant.
Me: I know.

Pete: Hear you're on the mend. Good. We miss you at the standardisation days.
Me: I miss the free biscuits.
Pete: Seriously, if you want to do any moderation work, there's a bit coming up. Remote.
Me: Keep me in mind, sitting down.

Minh: Mr Graham, my son has IELTS next month. Can you talk to him?
Me: Bring him round on Saturday. I'll sit and chat.
Minh: Thank you, I will bring mango.
Me: Mango is always welcome.

Clinic: Reminder: appointment 12 October, 9am. Please bring your exercise log.
Me: I will. My exercise log is mostly 'sat down.'
Clinic: Please do your best, Mr Hollis.
